REALTIME CONVERSATION

ANALYTICS REPORT

OpenAI Realtime API | Audio + Text Session

01 — SESSION OVERVIEW

This report provides a comprehensive analysis of a real-time conversational AI session, including token usage, cost efficiency, speech metrics, and quality insights. The session utilized the Realtime Audio + Text API with the alloy voice model.

02 — USAGE STATISTICS

The table below summarizes all token consumption and the associated cost for this session. Cached tokens represent previously processed context that was efficiently reused.

03 — TOKEN EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS

Input Composition

Output Composition

Audio tokens account for the majority of both input and output usage, which is expected for a real-time voice-based session. The high cached token count (4,672) indicates effective context reuse.

04 — ESTIMATED WORD COUNT ANALYSIS

Word counts are estimated from the assistant transcripts provided for this session. The session included multiple substantial explanatory responses.

Segment Breakdown

Speaker Summary

05 — PERFORMANCE METRICS

The assistant generated approximately 423 words over 60.15 seconds of audio output. The calculated speech rate is as follows:

06 — COST BREAKDOWN

The total session cost was $0.098375 USD — approximately 9.8 cents for a full-duplex real-time multimodal interaction lasting approximately 3 minutes.

07 — CONVERSATION QUALITY INSIGHTS

Strengths

Observations

09 — WHY INPUT TOKENS ARE HIGHER THAN OUTPUT

A common question when reviewing realtime session stats is: why are input tokens so much larger than output tokens? The answer lies in how the Realtime API constructs each request internally.

The Technical Reason

When a user says a single word — for example, Hello — the model does not receive just that word. Instead, every turn sends a far larger context package to the model. The actual input for each turn includes:

10 — AUDIO TOKEN EXPANSION

Audio is not tokenized the same way text is. A few spoken seconds can generate hundreds of audio tokens because the system must process far more information than a simple text string.

Text vs. Audio Token Comparison

What Audio Processing Includes

11 — INPUT TOKEN FORMULA & VISUAL BREAKDOWN

The total billed input tokens for each turn are not just the current user message. They represent the sum of every context component the API sends to the model:

Token Composition Formula

Text Chat vs. Realtime Voice — Side by Side

Your Session — Token Breakdown Explained

Final Conclusion

12 — TECHNICAL SUMMARY

The following JSON object provides a complete machine-readable summary of all session metrics for integration with downstream analytics or logging systems.

Table 9 columns: ℹ The elevated speech rate (~422 wpm) is typical of TTS systems, which compress natural pauses and deliver speech more densely than a human speaker.
ℹ Human conversational speech typically ranges between 120–180 wpm; TTS systems often exceed 300 wpm due to reduced hesitation and filler.

Table 10 columns: Resource | Contribution | Notes
Audio Processing | ~70–80% | Dominant cost driver
Text Generation | ~15–20% | Secondary cost factor
Cached Token Savings | Significant | 4,672 tokens reused

Table 11 columns: ✅ Cached tokens (4,672) significantly reduced compute cost by avoiding redundant context reprocessing.
✅ At under 10 cents for ~600 spoken words and real-time TTS/STT, this session demonstrates strong cost efficiency for multimodal AI.

Table 12 columns: ✅ Efficient cache utilization — 4,672 cached tokens reused, reducing cost and latency.
✅ Balanced audio and text usage maintained throughout the session.
✅ Low total cost relative to interaction depth and audio output volume.
✅ Good conversational continuity across topic transitions.
✅ Stable token growth pattern with no anomalous spikes.

Table 13 columns: ⚠ Audio tokens dominate total usage — as expected in voice-first sessions.
⚠ Long explanatory responses (e.g., geography and AI/ML segments) significantly increase audio token consumption.
⚠ Real-time voice responses consume tokens faster than text-only interactions due to TTS overhead.

Table 14 columns: System Prompt
Previous Messages
Conversation State
Audio Frames
Transcription Data
Session Metadata
Realtime Events
Current Audio Chunk

Table 15 columns: ℹ The OpenAI Realtime API keeps its own internal copy of the entire conversational history for a session. This single architectural decision is why input tokens accumulate rapidly across turns.

Table 16 columns: Input | Text Tokens | Audio Tokens
Saying "Hello" | 1-2 tokens | Dozens of tokens
Why? | Just characters | Waveform + timing + silence + phonetics + embeddings

Table 17 columns: 🔊 Waveform chunks — raw audio signal data sampled at high frequency.
⏱ Timing information — precise start and end timestamps for each utterance.
🔇 Silence detection — Voice Activity Detection (VAD) events that segment the audio.
🗣 Phonetic encoding — phoneme-level representations of speech sounds.
📐 Audio embeddings — high-dimensional vector representations of audio content.

Table 18 columns: Total Input Tokens =
 Current User Input
 + Conversation History (all previous turns)
 + System Prompt
 + Audio Chunks (current frame)
 + Session Metadata & VAD Events
 + Transcription Overhead
 
Output Tokens =
 Assistant Response Only

Table 19 columns: Text Chat | Realtime Voice Chat
User → small input
AI → medium output | Audio stream
+ history replay
+ system prompt
+ metadata
+ transcription
+ VAD events
+ cached context
= VERY LARGE input

Table 20 columns: ✅ input_tokens: 5,209 — elevated due to audio streaming, repeated context, system instructions, and transcription overhead.
✅ output_tokens: 3,754 — assistant response only; naturally lower than input.
✅ audio_tokens_in: 3,688 — user audio frames (waveform + VAD + phonetics).
✅ audio_tokens_out: 3,042 — TTS output audio for all assistant responses.
✅ cached_tokens: 4,672 — reused context, significantly reducing cost and latency.

Table 21 columns: 📌 Input tokens are higher than output tokens in realtime models because the API continuously sends accumulated conversation context, audio chunks, metadata, and system instructions back into the model for every turn.
✅ This behavior is expected, officially documented, and fundamental to how realtime conversational AI works.

}
